ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Participants were recruited via Prolific and compensated for their time.

> At the time of testing, participants were living in the United States and United Kingdom (L1 English), Germany and Austria (L1 German), or France (L1 French).

> Demographic details of the included participants are provided in Table 1.

> Participants were randomly assigned to one of the two lists and saw all items in that list.

> Following the acceptability judgement task, participants completed the LexTALE lexical decision test to obtain a measure of English proficiency.

> Finally, participants completed a demographic background questionnaire designed to collect information on dialect exposure and use in English.

> In total, the entire experiment took 30-40 minutes to complete, and participants were compensated after completing all tasks.

> That is, while many participants were primarily exposed to American English at the time of testing, the majority were educated in British English.

report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

live_data_statements: Participants were recruited via Prolific and compensated for their time.
At the time of testing, participants were living in the United States and United Kingdom (L1 English), Germany and Austria (L1 German), or France (L1 French).
Demographic details of the included participants are provided in Table 1.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of the two lists and saw all items in that list.
Following the acceptability judgement task, participants completed the LexTALE lexical decision test to obtain a measure of English proficiency.
Finally, participants completed a demographic background questionnaire designed to collect information on dialect exposure and use in English.
In total, the entire experiment took 30-40 minutes to complete, and participants were compensated after completing all tasks.
That is, while many participants were primarily exposed to American English at the time of testing, the majority were educated in British English.

info.title: Agreement with Collective Nouns in L2 English: Effects of Syntax, Dialect, and Frequency

text.text: Within the second language (L2) acquisition field, there is a large divide between generative/formal approaches and variationist approaches.
In this study, we attempt to unite these approaches by implementing a sociosyntactic approach which adopts aspects of both formal and variationist research.
Specifically, we examine the acquisition of verbal agreement with collective nouns by French and German learners of L2 English.
On the formal side, we investigate how universal restrictions on Agree, i.e., c-command, constrain the availability of plural agreement.
On the variationist side, we explore how differences in exposure to American vs.
British English affect the acceptance of plural agreement.
We find that plural agreement is largely rejected by both L2 groups.
Still, the German learners display sensitivity to the universal constraints on Agree.
While the French learners do not, their behavior also did not violate these constraints.
Furthermore, while we find an effect of dialect exposure, it was the opposite of what was predicted: those learners exposed to more American English rated plural agreement higher.
We ultimately argue that future research should continue to adopt the sociosyntactic approach to gain a fuller understanding of the L2 acquisition process.

Within the field of second language (L2) acquisition, there are two broad research paradigms: (1) generative/formal approaches (Slabakova, 2026; White, 2020; Rothman and Slabakova, 2018; and citations therein) and (2) variationist approaches (Gudmestad and Kanwit, 2025; Bayley and Escalante, 2022; and citations therein).
text.formatted: Within the field of second language (L2) acquisition, there are two broad research paradigms: (1) generative/formal approaches <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Slabakova, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">White, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Rothman and Slabakova, 2018</ref>; and citations therein) and (2) variationist approaches <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Gudmestad and Kanwit, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Bayley and Escalante, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">and citations therein)</ref>.

text.text: While both approaches seek to address questions central to L2 learners' linguistic competence, there is little (joint) work between the two traditions, as they are often viewed as complementary, and sometimes even in opposition.
This division is due to the questions that each addresses.
The generative approach to L2 acquisition has largely investigated the role of innate language-specific mechanisms in additional language acquisition.

Still, within this field there is a growing body of work that addresses the role of extra-linguistic factors, such as frequency, in interaction with these linguistic mechanisms (e.g., Smeets, 2024; Slabakova, 2015; Gonzalez, 2023; Rankin and Wagner, 2025; and many others).
text.formatted: Still, within this field there is a growing body of work that addresses the role of extra-linguistic factors, such as frequency, in interaction with these linguistic mechanisms (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Smeets, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Slabakova, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Gonzalez, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Rankin and Wagner, 2025</ref>; and many others).

text.text: Variationist approaches, on the other hand, largely address contexts of language use, particularly in relation to sociolinguistic variables, such as age, gender, and region (e.g., Geeslin and Gudmestad, 2010, 2016; Regan and Terry, 2025).
text.formatted: Variationist approaches, on the other hand, largely address contexts of language use, particularly in relation to sociolinguistic variables, such as age, gender, and region (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Geeslin and</ref> <ref type="bibr">Gudmestad, 2010, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Regan and Terry, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, this subfield has generally not addressed the role of a language faculty in additional language acquisition.
A similar divide is found in the general linguistics literature.

However, in theoretical linguistics work, there have been significant attempts to unite the two approaches, with theoretical discussion devoted to questions of syntactic variation (e.g. Cornips and Corrigan, 2005; Adger and Trousdale, 2007; Duncan and Robinson, 2025).
text.formatted: However, in theoretical linguistics work, there have been significant attempts to unite the two approaches, with theoretical discussion devoted to questions of syntactic variation (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Cornips and Corrigan, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Adger and Trousdale, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Duncan and Robinson, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This has given rise to the field of sociosyntax, which is situated at the intersection of generative syntax and variationist sociolinguistics.

That is, this framework seeks to address both what the set of possible utterances are and the restrictions on them, in alignment with the generative tradition, as well as the factors that influence the use and frequency of occurrence of those utterances, in alignment with the variationist tradition.
In this study, we apply the sociosyntactic framework to L2 acquisition.
Specifically, we examine how a universal syntactic mechanism, Agree, constrains the occurrence of variability between semantic and syntactic verbal agreement with collective nouns in L2 English.

In conjunction with this more generative/formal investigation, we explore how differences in the frequency of this variation in agreement across dialects, as well as differences in exposure to those dialects by L2 learners, leads to differences in the acceptance of the variant.
We characterize research on variability in L2 acquisition in generative and variationist SLA as reflecting differences in focus and emphasis, rather than necessarily a fundamental divide.
Applying sociosyntactic thinking, we incorporate elements of each into consideration of the acquisition of the linguistic variable of agreement with collective nouns in English.
Generative SLA has a long tradition of research on variability, even if it has typically adopted different terminology.

The focus has been on syntactic 'optionality' and research has investigated the extent to which operations which give rise to optionality are subject to similar constraints in L1 and L2 speakers, and the extent to which L1 influence is at play in the occurrence of this optionality (e.g., Unsworth, 2004; Hopp, 2005; etc.).
text.formatted: The focus has been on syntactic 'optionality' and research has investigated the extent to which operations which give rise to optionality are subject to similar constraints in L1 and L2 speakers, and the extent to which L1 influence is at play in the occurrence of this optionality (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Unsworth, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Hopp, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr">etc.</ref>).

text.text: A central focus has been word order and the interfaces of syntax with semantics and pragmatics, with an influential proposal being that optionality at the end-state of very advanced L2 acquisition is the result of the interface of syntax with pragmatics (e.g., Sorace, 2011).
text.formatted: A central focus has been word order and the interfaces of syntax with semantics and pragmatics, with an influential proposal being that optionality at the end-state of very advanced L2 acquisition is the result of the interface of syntax with pragmatics (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Sorace, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: For example, pronominal subjects in Italian may be null or post-verbal, in addition to overt pre-verbal expression.
The felicity of use of null/post-verbal subjects is regulated by discourse-pragmatic factors such as topic and focus.

Italian contrasts with English, which does not syntactically license null or post-verbal subjects, where the distinction between the two languages is traditionally viewed as opposite settings of a null-subject parameter.
Studies have shown that even advanced L1 English-L2 Italian speakers evidence optionality in their production and judgement of null/post-verbal subjects in Italian (e.g., Belletti et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Studies have shown that even advanced L1 English-L2 Italian speakers evidence optionality in their production and judgement of null/post-verbal subjects in Italian (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Belletti et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, Sorace (2011) argues that this optionality is not a syntactic issue.
text.formatted: Nevertheless, <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Sorace (2011)</ref> argues that this optionality is not a syntactic issue.

text.text: Rather, the learners have acquired the grammar of null subjects; however, knowing when to felicitously use them in context remains a persistent challenge.
Extra-linguistic issues regarding exposure, frequency, and input, in interaction with linguistic constraints, are seen as central to explaining these learning outcomes.
To illustrate, Slabakova (2015) tests focus fronting, topicalization and clitic left dislocation (CLLD) in L2 Spanish and L2 English.
text.formatted: To illustrate, <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Slabakova (2015)</ref> tests focus fronting, topicalization and clitic left dislocation (CLLD) in L2 Spanish and L2 English.

text.text: While these interface properties are all regulated by discourseappropriateness, the key difference between them is construction frequency interacting with transfer: focus fronting is available in both languages, CLLD is restricted to Spanish but is frequent in speech across all varieties, and topicalization is available in English but exceedingly rare.
While learners of Spanish show robust knowledge of CLLD, learners of English even at near-native levels do not show knowledge of topicalization.
The learnability issue is not simply integrating information at the syntax-pragmatics interface, but rather the interplay of input frequency, L1 transfer (and UG).

Variationist SLA, on the other hand, puts extra-linguistic variables center-stage and investigates L2 sociolinguistic development in terms of probabilistic, socially meaningful patterns of use (see Geeslin, 2018; Regan and Terry, 2025).
text.formatted: Variationist SLA, on the other hand, puts extra-linguistic variables center-stage and investigates L2 sociolinguistic development in terms of probabilistic, socially meaningful patterns of use (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Geeslin, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Regan and Terry, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The focus is on language production, unlike generative SLA's aim to abstract away from performance.

However, in line with the variationist tradition, variable usage is not assumed to be a poor reflection of underlying competence, but rather indicative of the "orderly heterogeneity" of language use in context (Weinreich et al., 1968).
text.formatted: However, in line with the variationist tradition, variable usage is not assumed to be a poor reflection of underlying competence, but rather indicative of the "orderly heterogeneity" of language use in context <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Weinreich et al., 1968)</ref>.

text.text: Studies of L2 variation show how this orderly heterogeneity plays out in learners' performance.
Pertinent illustration comes from studies of subject expression in L2 Spanish for which the acquisition of null subjects is also investigated (e.g., Geeslin and Gudmestad, 2010, 2016).
text.formatted: Pertinent illustration comes from studies of subject expression in L2 Spanish for which the acquisition of null subjects is also investigated (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Geeslin and</ref> <ref type="bibr">Gudmestad, 2010, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: This variationist work surveys the full range of ways in which native and non-native speakers of Spanish can express subjects according to linguistic constraints such as person, number, discourse status, and so on.
This variable production is then also analyzed against a range of sociodemographic factors such as age, gender, time spent abroad, and identity.

This examination delivers sociolinguistic findings such as the fact that subject-expression among native speakers of Spanish is affected by speaker gender, but not among L2 speakers (Geeslin and Gudmestad, 2010).
text.formatted: This examination delivers sociolinguistic findings such as the fact that subject-expression among native speakers of Spanish is affected by speaker gender, but not among L2 speakers <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Geeslin and Gudmestad, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, from a linguistic perspective, L1 and L2 speakers produce similar rates of null and overt pronouns in first person contexts, but their rates differ significantly for second person pronouns, where L1 speakers use more personal pronouns than L2 learners (Geeslin and Gudmestad, 2016).
text.formatted: Additionally, from a linguistic perspective, L1 and L2 speakers produce similar rates of null and overt pronouns in first person contexts, but their rates differ significantly for second person pronouns, where L1 speakers use more personal pronouns than L2 learners <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Geeslin and Gudmestad, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Despite differences in underlying theoretical assumptions and methodological choices, we can identify a certain overlap in concerns of generative and variationist SLA, especially as regards questions of linguistic exposure and experience in the development of an L2.
In our study, we take a sociosyntactic perspective by focusing on formal learnability considerations, considering issues of sociolinguistic variation in the input available to learners.
We treat verbal agreement with collective nouns in English as a linguistic variable, i.e. "alternative ways of 'saying the same thing'" (Labov, 1972: 94).
text.formatted: We treat verbal agreement with collective nouns in English as a linguistic variable, i.e. "alternative ways of 'saying the same thing'" <ref type="bibr">(Labov, 1972: 94)</ref>.

text.text: As will be discussed in the following section, this variation is constrained by linguistic and extralinguistic factors.
The resulting picture forms a learnability issue for learners of English whose L1s have different superficial agreement patterns.
Considering the (socio)linguistic variability in the input, we investigate learner preferences for semantic vs. syntactic agreement patterns, as conditioned by dialect exposure.

Collective nouns in English display variability in verbal agreement, allowing the occurrence of both singular and plural morphology (1; Quirk et al., 1985; Levin, 2001; Huddleston and Pullum, 2002; Hristov, 2013; among many others).

text.text: This is in opposition to other types of nouns, including general singular (2) and plural (3) nouns, which do not display such variability.
This variability in agreement morphology with collective nouns is linked to the choice between semantic and syntactic agreement.
Semantically, collective nouns are plural because they refer to groups of individuals or objects.
Syntactically, however, collective nouns are singular.
Therefore, when semantic agreement occurs, plural morphology appears, but when syntactic agreement occurs, singular morphology surfaces.
Other nouns do not have a mismatch between semantics and syntax, so variability never arises.
(1) The committee {was / were} considering her fate.
(2) A man {was / *were} considering her fate.
(3) The members of the committee {*was / were} considering her fate.

While agreement variability with collective nouns is observed across the major English dialects (Levin, 2001 (Levin, , 2006;; Bauer, 1988; Corbett, 2000), there is variation in the occurrence of semantic agreement between these dialects.

text.text: For example, Levin (2001) observes that plural morphology is produced much more frequently in British English than in American English.

text.text: Levin finds that plural morphology is produced about 23 percent of the time in British English, but it is only produced in about 3 percent of cases in American English.
However, there were additional effects of modality (written vs. spoken) and register (formal vs. informal).
Furthermore, even among the collective nouns there is variation in the frequency of production of plural morphology.

Levin, for example, finds that nouns referring to decision-making bodies (e.g., committee) tend to be used more with singular morphology, and more quantificational nouns tend to be used more with plural morphology (e.g., majority).
Still, there are collective nouns that were more clearly variable which did not belong to either type (e.g., family).
In addition to these factors, the use of singular and plural morphology with collective nouns is likely affected by other sociolinguistic variables as well.
There are, however, some syntactic restrictions on this variability.

Specifically, while both semantic and syntactic agreement may occur when collective nouns are pre-verbal (1), when collective nouns occur in existential constructions, plural agreement becomes impossible (4; Elbourne, 1999; Munn, 1999; Smith, 2017; den Dikken, 2026).

text.text: Under this analysis, collective nouns carry two features: an uninterpretable singular feature and an interpretable plural feature.

For evidence that nouns may carry non-matching features for the same construct, comparisons are drawn with pluralia tantum nouns (e.g., scissors), which are argued to carry an uninterpretable plural feature and an interpretable singular feature, and cases of gender mismatch, as with German Mädchen ('girl'), which carries an uninterpretable neuter feature and an interpretable feminine feature.
Importantly, Smith shows that Agree can target either the interpretable or the uninterpretable feature, though there are some restrictions on this optionality.
Semantic agreement occurs when the interpretable feature is accessed, and syntactic agreement when the uninterpretable feature is accessed.

Leaving aside some of the details of how this achieved, it is argued that "[semantic agreement] requires the controller to c-command the target at LF, but [syntactic agreement] does not" (Smith, 2017: 827).

As collective nouns c-command the verb when they are pre-verbal subjects, both types of agreement can occur.

text.text: Turning to the current study, L1 French and German learners of English are expected to display different acquisition paths.

At the initial state, due to (full) transfer (Schwartz and Sprouse, 1996), the L1 French learners are expected to accept semantic agreement with (at least some) collective nouns, but the L1 German learners are expected to reject this agreement.

text.text: However, both groups should behave the same regarding the rejection of semantic agreement in existential clauses, due to universal restrictions on Agree, despite the lack of evidence from L1 influence and the lack of negative evidence in the input regarding the impossibility of semantic agreement in existential clauses (i.e., encountering syntactic agreement does not rule out the possibility of semantic agreement, and this specific property is not taught), assuming full access to domain-specific linguistic mechanisms (Schwartz and Sprouse, 1996).

text.text: Additionally, both groups' acceptance of semantic agreement with collective nouns will likely be affected by their sociolinguistic experience.
Differing rates of exposure to specific English dialects will provide different amounts of positive evidence for grammar restructuring.
For the L1 French learners, this adjustment would consist of lowering acceptance for those exposed to more American English or increasing acceptance for those exposed to more British English.

For the L1 German learners, exposure to both dialects should prompt increased acceptance of semantic agreement, though this adjustment will likely be more readily facilitated for those exposed to British English more.
In this study we address the acquisition of semantic agreement with collective nouns by L1 French and German learners of L2 English.
We address the following research questions: 1.
Do L2 English learners accept semantic agreement with collective nouns?
We expect a proficiency effect.
As proficiency increases, the L1 German learners will begin to accept semantic agreement, but the L1 French learners should accept it from the initial state.

Because of the higher frequency of semantic agreement with collective nouns in British English, those with greater (relative) exposure to British English will begin to accept semantic agreement earlier than those with greater exposure to American English.
Are L2 English learners sensitive to the syntactic restrictions on semantic agreement?

As the syntactic restriction is a universal constraint on Agree, we predict learners will be sensitive to this restriction from the earliest stages of acquisition, even though their L1s do not provide evidence for its application in the tested context.

It is important to test L1 English speakers' sensitivity to this restriction as well to create a baseline to compare the L2 learners' behavior with because the application of this restriction has not been empirically tested previously.
Does learner knowledge of agreement align with their sociolinguistic experience in the rates of exposure to different varieties?
We predict that with increasing proficiency, learners will converge on dialect-specific acceptance patterns.

As English learners are often exposed to both American and British dialects, the effect will depend on the dialect they are primarily exposed to; that is, the relative proportion of exposure should influence the speed of convergence.

For example, those exposed to a higher proportion of British English will accept semantic agreement more than those exposed to a higher proportion of American English, and this should begin at lower proficiency levels.
Again, it is important to test L1 English speakers' judgements of semantic agreement as well to determine whether they align with dialectal differences in production frequency.
Data were collected from 32 L1 English, 37 L1 German/L2 English, and 36 L1 French/L2 English participants.
Participants were recruited via Prolific and compensated for their time.
At the time of testing, participants were living in the United States and United Kingdom (L1 English), Germany and Austria (L1 German), or France (L1 French).
To participate, individuals were required to be at least 18 years old.

Additionally, the L2 English learner groups were required to have acquired English strictly as their L2, i.e., as the first language they acquired after their L1, but they were not restricted regarding having acquired any further languages following the onset of English acquisition.
Simultaneous bilinguals (multiple L1s) were not included in this study.
Additionally, the L1 English group was not restricted regarding languages acquired sequentially after the L1 (i.e., L2+), but simultaneous bilinguals were not included.

text.text: The LexTALE scores indicate high-intermediate to advanced proficiency levels for both L2 groups, and there is significant variation within the groups.
The distribution of LexTALE scores was not normally distributed based on a Shapiro-Wilk Test (p = .012), so non-parametric tests were used.

A Kruskall-Wallis H Test indicates that there is a significant difference in LexTALE scores between groups: χ 2 (2) = 7.57, p = .023, with a mean rank score of 65.28 for the L1 English group, 48.50 for the L1 German group, and 46.71 for the L1 French group.

The Post-Hoc Dunn's test using a Bonferroni-corrected alpha of 0.017 indicated that the mean rank of the L1 English group is significantly higher than both the L1 German (p = .022) and L1 French groups (p = .012), but the L1 French and L1 German groups were not significantly different (p = .801).
We conducted an acceptability judgement task (AJT) testing acceptance of verbal agreement with collective nouns in two conditions: structure (SV, VS_wh, VS_there) and agreement (syntactic, semantic).
Here, SV refers to sentences in which the collective noun is pre-verbal.
In VS_wh items, the collective noun is post-verbal in wh-questions, but still located in the TP, where it c-commands the verb at LF.
In VS_there items, the collective noun is post-verbal due to being part of an existential clause.
These conditions were fully crossed.
Responses were rated on a scale of 1-4, where 4 indicated 'Completely Acceptable' and 1 'Completely Unacceptable'.
Labels were always presented with the response scale.

In this study we examined the acquisition of variability in syntactic and semantic agreement with collective nouns in English by L1 French and German learners.
In doing so, we addressed the role of syntactic environment (i.e., licit vs. illicit) in the acceptance of the two types of agreement.

Additionally, we examined the effect of differences in the relative frequency of semantic agreement compared to syntactic agreement in American and British English, in combination with learners' exposure to those dialects, in the acceptance of semantic agreement.
In analyzing the effects of both formal (i.e., generative) and sociolinguistic (i.e., variationist) aspects of semantic agreement, we adopted a sociosyntactic approach to L2 acquisition.
Returning to our research questions, we first asked whether the L2 learners accept semantic agreement with collective nouns.

Contrary to our predictions, the learners did not tend to accept semantic agreement; that is, there is little evidence for the acceptance of semantic agreement by either L1 group at any proficiency level.
Additionally, the learners' acceptance of semantic agreement tends to decrease as their proficiency in English increases, regardless of L1 background.

This general lack of acceptance by both groups, while not surprising for the L1 German group at lower proficiency levels, is surprising for the L1 French group who could potentially transfer semantic agreement with predicates from their L1.
It is possible that such transfer was not more evident because of the nouns chosen in this experiment.

While French speakers produce semantic agreement with more quantificational collective nouns (see, e.g., Tristram, 2014), we are unaware of data on the occurrence of semantic agreement with less quantificational nouns like team and family, which were the type primarily used in this study.
A future study should examine the granularity of transfer by examining the acceptance of semantic agreement with quantificational vs. non-quantificational nouns by L1 French/L2 English learners.

Though our study was not designed to differentiate these collective noun types, preliminary positive evidence is found with the SV structure, such that the average rating of semantic agreement for quantificational nouns was higher than for non-quantificational nouns among the L1 French learners.

Notably, a similar difference was not found among the L1 German learners, suggesting that the patterns observed for the French can be viewed as evidence for the relexification approach to transfer (Sprouse, 2006).
text.formatted: Notably, a similar difference was not found among the L1 German learners, suggesting that the patterns observed for the French can be viewed as evidence for the relexification approach to transfer <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Sprouse, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: That is, individual lexical items are transferred with their associated features (however construed) and the learner maps those features to a lexical item in the input.
Our second research question addressed L1 English speakers' and L2 English learners' sensitivity to syntactic restrictions on semantic agreement.
Both groups of L1 English speakers display sensitivity to the restriction on semantic agreement.
For the British English speakers, this sensitivity is very clear.
For the American English speakers, the effect is less robust because there was no difference in their ratings between VS_wh and VS_there sentences.
However, this lack of robustness is likely due to floor effects.
The L1 German learners also display some sensitivity to the restriction on semantic agreement because they rate VS_there sentences lower than SV sentences.
As with the American English speakers, however, they did not differentiate the VS_wh and VS_there contexts.
Again, though, this lack of difference is likely a floor effect.

Finally, the L1 French learners did not show any evidence of sensitivity to the syntactic restriction as none of the contexts produced statistically different ratings, though they also did not violate the restriction because they tended to reject all semantic agreement.
So, again, there were floor effects.

These findings are consistent with the prediction that semantic agreement in contexts where the subject does not c-command the verb will be rejected both initially and at all proficiency levels by the L2 acquirers because it is a universal constraint on possible grammars (e.g., Smith, 2017).

text.text: This knowledge is available in the L2 despite the lack of evidence available from their L1 grammars, which either never display semantic agreement with collective nouns (German) or only have invariant agreement morphology in existential clauses (French).
Our final research question asked whether there were effects of English dialect (exposure) on the acceptance/rating of semantic agreement.
There are clear differences in the acceptance patterns by L1 speakers of the two English dialects.
The British English speakers did not make a distinction between syntactic and semantic agreement in licit syntactic contexts in their ratings, strongly accepting both types of agreement.
The American English speakers, however, rated syntactic agreement higher in both licit syntactic contexts.

Additionally, while the two groups never differed in their ratings for syntactic agreement, the British English speakers provided higher ratings than the American English speakers for semantic agreement in both licit syntactic contexts.

The rating patterns correspond to the previously observed frequency differences between American and British English in the frequency of production of semantic agreement with collective nouns: British English speakers both produce semantic agreement more, and rate it higher, than American English speakers.
We also found effects of dialect exposure among the L2 learners.

However, contrary to our predictions, the more a learner reported exposure to American English (compared to British English), the more likely they were to accept semantic agreement (in the SV syntactic context for all learners, and generally for L1 German speakers.
This finding is surprising because the frequency of occurrence of semantic agreement in British English is much higher than in American English.
Additionally, the L1 English speakers' judgement behavior mirrors the general frequency data.

It is possible that the dialect differences observed for the frequency of semantic agreement in L1 corpora do not match the input that the L2 learners are exposed to; however, it would be odd to find that L2-directed input from American English speakers would contain more evidence of semantic agreement than L2-directed input from British English speakers.
Given this, the unexpected direction of dialect exposure effects should be addressed in future studies with other dialect-specific properties.
It is also possible that while relative exposure points towards influence from one dialect, cumulative exposure would paint another picture.
That is, while many participants were primarily exposed to American English at the time of testing, the majority were educated in British English.
Potentially, this early input had a more significant impact on the acquisition process than current exposure.

Research on other L2s, principally Spanish, shows that dialect exposure, even in an immersion setting during study abroad does not reliably result in acquisition of sociolinguistically constrained grammatical variables (e.g., Linford, 2016; papers in Zahler et al., 2023).

text.text: The nature of the linguistic variable and individual differences such as identity and attitudes also play a role.
This is even more challenging in the L2 English context, where the status of English means that input to individual L2 speakers likely comes from a range of both L1 and L2 varieties.
For formal approaches to language acquisition, this raises some questions about the nature of the "target" grammar.
Clearly, future research should continue to explore methods of accounting for variation in exposure and how this relates to L2 acquisition outcomes even within a formalist framework.
This study is a first attempt to adopt a sociosyntactic framework in L2 acquisition, marrying questions about formal learnability to issues of sociolinguistic patterns in the input.
Future studies should expand on this endeavor by examining further linguistic properties where sociolinguistically relevant variation and universal mechanisms interact.
While here we examined variation in frequency across dialects/regions, one could also explore other sociolinguistic variables, such as age, gender, prestige, and L2-self.
Furthermore, in this study we only examined effects of learners' relative exposure to the written form of different dialects on the acceptance of semantic agreement.
Future studies could also consider other measures of exposure, such as exposure to spoken dialects and calculations of total input, rather than relative measures.

One could also explore other potential predictors that are otherwise related to dialect exposure, such as motivation to sound/write like a particular dialect speaker, the dialect that was taught in formal lessons, identity and attitudes toward a dialect, the role of close contacts who are speakers of particular dialects, and immersion experience within specific dialect areas (e.g., Gudmestad and Kanwit, 2025; and citations therein).

text.text: Additionally, one could create and/or search a corpus of L2-directed input to determine how the frequency of semantic agreement differs from L1-directed speech/writing.

Research on wider variation beyond American and British English, such as in outer-circle varieties (e.g., Hundt, 2006), suggests that the available input is messier, and leads to more diverse acquisition outcomes, than what has been considered within the L2 literature so far.
